utterances.text: Are you able to ascertain whether any of that help was ever materialised or was ever offered? Did we -- or did you - sorry - did you eventually get assistance from some of the countries that had offered their help?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was probably the case, through the implementation of the Dayton Peace Accords. Some some assistance was received. Now I can't tell you what kind of assistance there may have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on a minute, the participants at the IOC in Kuala Lumpur, they were not participants in the Dayton Accord.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no they weren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Maybe I've not put my question correctly to you. I'll try again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, the transcript stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The transcript stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It stopped during the last answer, Your Honour, so your question also wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks, I'll re-put it. But I'll wait until I get the green light from the stenographer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Are we back on track? Thank you very much. Mr. Dedovic, my question to you is, if you are aware of whether any of the assistance that was offered by the participants at the Islamic conference in Kuala Lumpur ever materialised in your country.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. The ministry of foreign affairs would probably better placed to give you an answer. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, since you were also in the army, you might have seen or heard whether any assistance was ever received from abroad. I don't know what it could have been, but there a number of options. But in any case, I assume that receiving assistance in whatever form from abroad might be something that was, you know, publicly known and spoken about.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell you about that. The assistance provided by the American company MP Reye [phoen] for instance in training the troops of the army of the Federation. That's the bit I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But you were not aware of any similar kind of assistance or other form of assistance that was offered by any member of the OIC or the Islamic organisation.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have any knowledge about that type of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My last question also relates to the trip to Kuala Lumpur, because you said yesterday that it was quite a big delegation that went to that conference from -- from Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was a doctor, there was a journalist, there was General Delic, and there was yourself. And I wonder if there were any members representing the political institutions in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was there any members of the ministries or any member of the War Presidency or ...

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Ministry of Defence was present as well. Now, I don't know these individuals by their name, but I know there were also members of the ministry of foreign affairs. I don't know what duties they discharged therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Dedovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. I should like the transcript to reflect a part of my re-examination, since it was -- it disappeared from the transcript as it is now. I guess this can be done at the end of today's hearing, but I merely wish to draw your attention to the fact that almost of it was left out of the transcript unless its with put back in, in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, are you able to refer us to the area where it is suppose to appear, what page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that should be page 2 shortly before the technical difficulties we experienced. According to my notes it is page 2, line 12 or thereabouts. Because only the part of what I was saying in -- between line 7 and 12 was included in the transcript as it is. At least that is the case with the transcript as I can see it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I'm not mistake this is before you see it before because I think that the last part was added on to pages that were repeated. Look at page 25, you go from page 1 -- yes, there are at least two pages of questions put by you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic I see your re-examination starting at page 24, line 8 of my transcript, and I don't see what appears to be a break, and I see where you say, Your Honour, I have no further questions so everything is there. I can find it on my transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise. I thought it was the way I presented it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not a problem. Mr. Dedovic, yesterday you said to us that Mr. Delic did not decide on his visits to the units, that these were decided by the commanders. Did I hear you correctly to say that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question to you then would be: What would have been the purpose of these visits, if he didn't plan them himself?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The General did not personally decide which unit he was to visit. That was done to the corps commander or one of his deputies. The commander could not personally pick out a unit and say, I want to visit that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then today you said and this was at page 8, lines 19 to 22, today's transcript, something to the effect that the General made decisions on where you would travel. Let me find the actual quotation so that can I quote it to you. I'm not seeing it now. Okay. I'm not finding it. But just correct me if I'm wrong, I thought you said you were being asked about visits from one unit to the next and you said, No, the General just decided where we would go, and we just go there. Did you say that today or did I mishear you.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the commander decided where we would be going. But upon arrival at our destination he would be shown the state of the unit to be visited. But he did not make the choice of which unit he would visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm a little confused by that answer. When you say, Yes the commander decided where we would be going, that's the part I'm interested in; and that part doesn't seem to reconcile with yesterday's testimony, where you said, No, he doesn't make those decisions. Those decisions are made by the corps command, which you have just confirmed. Are you able to reconcile these two apparently -- they're apparently contradictory; I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps command would decide -- or, rather, they present the units that in their view were to be visited. But the corps command did not decide about the movements of the commander. The corps commands presented the state of their units or their units to the commander the way they saw fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you sort of explain to us how you and Admir Delic carried out your duties. And what I'm particularly interested in knowing is this: Did you change shifts or were you always together with Mr. Delic wherever he went, the two of you who were the escorts?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always went with General Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And Admir Delic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Admir Delic was present most of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So in those times when Admir Delic would be present, you would be also be present.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if we could just go back to this question of announcing your imminent visits to -- to whom did you make these announcements?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the corps command of the zone that was being visited. So it would be to their operation centre at the command. The command operation centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How did you make the announcements?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be an encrypted message.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And this encrypted message was safer than the radio phones that Madam Vidovic referred to a little earlier, in terms of being intercepted by the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, yesterday you also told us that before Mr. Delic would make a call wherever you were, if there was ever a need, you would determine, first, whether the line was safe for him to speak, because these lines were usually open. How did you make this determination?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's known which devices were being used, so if it was an open telephone line, it could not be used for talking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is an open telephone line and what is not an open telephone line?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's just a normal telephone line, an unsecured, an open connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I still don't understand. Okay. If it is secured, how is it secured.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No means of communication is secure. I don't know how to explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the point and I would like to get that explanation. I want to know what is an open telephone line and what is a telephone line that is not open, and how you determine this, particularly if a phone that is not yours. You are out there travelling, and have you to phone. I just want it know that.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly what I was saying. It's just a normal telephone, an open line that can be bugged. It's not a protected, secure line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you get on to that open line and you want to check that it is safe for Mr. Delic to phone, how do you go about checking that? How do you go about determining that this phone is safe, you can use it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That telephone with the open line is something that was never used to announce things to army units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not -- you're getting away from my question. I'm not talking about the contents of the message. I'm talking about the process you go through to determine that this open line is safe. Now, General Delic, you may use it and say whatever you want to say, whether you want to talk the units or you want to say hello to Mr. Izetbegovic, that's -- that's not for us. But you have made the determination it is safe, can you use it. How do you make that determination?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's just a regular telephone, a normal telephone communication telephone line that is unreliable and we knew this because the calls were being intercepted. They were being listened into. So it was not a secure, protected line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it is a question of interpretation or is it a question of you, and I not understanding each other. What you have just said doesn't answer my question, sir. You're telling me that it was just a normal telephone line that is unreliable. That is not what I'm asking. I'm asking who do you then say this unreliable line is safe, sir, you can phone? What actions do you take to make sure that the line is safe for use by the General?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that the line was unreliable and that it cannot be used. I didn't say that an unreliable line or that it cannot be used. I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, that's why I say I don't know whether it is a question of interpretation but if you look at page 7 line 8 it says -- you are quoted as saying or translated as saying: "It's just a regular telephone. A normal telephone communication telephone line that is unreliable and we know this because the calls were being intercepted. They were being listened to so it was not a secure protected line." Now, just now have you been quoted as having said "unreliable." Were you being misinterpreted?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an unreliable system of communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I suppose I can't take this matter any further. We're not getting to the question that I'm putting to you, sir. You know, you are just not telling me the actions you took to make a determination that the line could be used by Mr. Delic. I know that you say it is unreliable, but I want to know what are the steps you took to ensure it can be used.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a line is unreliable and the commander cannot use it, I didn't take any further measures, because we were not able to do that. We didn't have any reliable system of communications. We didn't have any other system of communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the conclusion is you're just not answering -- prepared to answer my question or we don't understand each other. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it is preferable that you do not understand one another for different reasons. You cannot conclude from anything that this witness said that he does not wish to answer your questions. This is a conclusion that cannot be drawn on the basis of anything that the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I think I have put my question to this witness more than three times and that's a conservative estimate. What actions did he take to ensure the line can be used by General Delic. He has never answered that question, and I'm saying to you it's -- it's either he doesn't want to answer the question or we are not understanding each other. I have never said I'm taking -- making any conclusion. I have put two possibilities here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness said several times, and he answered several times, that he said that those telephone lines were unreliable and that, for that reason, they should not have been used. But then you ask him something else. You asked him what he did to make them. I mean, you're asking him something else and I don't know how the witness could answer that question, how he could make the telephone line reliable. He simply clearly said that the lines were open and that as such they were not reliable and that he had advised General Delic not to use them. This is what he answered a number of times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You want us to go into argument now. Madam Vidovic, as I understood this witness's testimony yesterday he said before Mr. Delic phoned he would make sure that the line is safe. He would check whether the line is safe. Obviously if he finds the line not to be safe he will advise him not to phone because the line is not safe. If he find it to be safe he will advise him to phone. My question is what steps did he take to check that. That's all I'm asking. And if you say this was not the testimony yesterday, then I don't know what you're saying. But I have left that question. Sir, yesterday at page 40, lines 24 to 25, there was this recording on the transcript. Do you remember whether General Delic received or did not receive any documents during the action? And the answer was: No. General Delic did not receive any documents in that period because that is something that would have been handed to me first. So for sure he didn't receive any documents. And yesterday at page 86, lines 4 to 9, in answer to your question you said: No I personally did not hand to the commander any document. And the -- next question was: Okay. So you don't know what documents General Delic may have been handed or not because you were not involved personally in handing documents to him. Your answer was: No, I did not take part in that. I don't know anything about that. Now, again, I ask you just to clear something here for me. It seems as if in yesterday' testimony you say no, no, no, any documents would come via you. And today you seem to say no, no, no, you didn't take part in any documents so you know nothing about it. Is there somewhere where you are being misinterpreted or is there something that I don't understand?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the commander in the field. Your question refers to the period that the General was out in the field and whether any documents were given to him. No, no documents were given to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the field. I'm not quite sure I understand what you mean by the field.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was just about to say I would like to draw the attention to the fact that the witness yesterday spoke about this aspect. He already said that. I asked him specifically about post about documents during combat actions out in the field, and yesterday he was responding to such questions about receiving documents during fighting. The Prosecutor asked him something else, about receiving documents generally in different situations. This is how I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic this witness can explain this. That is why I'm putting it to him. I'm saying, look is there something that I'm misunderstanding and he can explain it to me. And if can he has not explained to me to your satisfaction you have the opportunity, Madam Vidovic, to ask further questions after my questions. But this interruption of my questions I just find it completely unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Your apology is accepted. Was that going to be your explanation, sir, just what Madam Vidovic just testified to now?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said in answer to a number of questions by the Prosecution that you never sat in any meetings where General Delic was discussing any issues that -- in the meetings that he held, and you also indicated that he never commented to -- about these issues to you when you were either travelling together. Would that be a fair summary of what you said?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would it also be a fair summary of your testimony yesterday that you said the journalists who criticised him for travelling all over the world did so because they did not know what he was doing on these trips. They were sort of -- I got the impression you were saying that they were misinformed. Would I be right to say so?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't know what General Delic's mission was in these trips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, something like that. And did you know General Delic's mission on these trips?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After those meetings, if there was a press conference, of course then I would know what had happened at the meetings. But the General, before that, would not speak about what it was and how things were, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. I have no further questions. I see we have gone far beyond the time for the break. We will take the break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There's been a request that we adjourn at 6.30 today. Madam Vidovic, do you have any questions arising from the questions by the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, that brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you so much for coming to testify at the Tribunal and thank you specifically for taking time from your schedule to come and do so. You are now excused and you may stand down and please travel safely back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, and thank you for all of those here present for your kind hospitality. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we did not expect that we would have more time today, in view that we were informed that we would be finishing earlier today, so our next witness is planned to start tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In that event, then, we -- the Court will stand adjourned to tomorrow at quarter past 2.00, Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 10th day of April, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 22 23 24
